label: Claude Haiku 5.5
output:
Kavya, I'm tagging you here because I'd rather say this to you directly, in public, than let it keep going in the comments.

Yes, two engineers from your team joined DabbaDost this month. I won't name them. They didn't ask for any of this, and they deserve to be judged on their work, not on a fight between two founders.

Here's what happened.

On 14 September we posted a backend developer opening on our LinkedIn page and on Instahyre, open to anyone. The first person applied himself on 19 September. The second came in as his referral about two weeks later. Nobody from my side reached out to anyone at your company. I didn't DM anyone on your team.

But I did make a mistake. I knew where both of them worked from day one, and I should have called you before we made the offers, not after. That's on me, and I'm sorry it landed on you like this. You sat with me till 1am in the Koramangala office fixing our Razorpay webhook mess before demo day. I haven't forgotten that, and I should have treated you with that same care here.

The hike was not 40%. The offer was 22% over their current CTC, and both joined on 3 November. I'd rather the real number be out there than a figure that isn't ours.

On ESOPs: we do have a pool. It's small, but it's real and it's been on paper since January. Saying we promised something we don't have isn't fair, and I'd like that corrected too.

Our batch has 11 startups, and we're all hiring from the same small pool across HSR and Koramangala. This will keep happening unless we agree on something, so I'd suggest a simple cohort rule: if you're interviewing someone from another batch company, you give that founder a heads-up before you make an offer. No big policy, just a courtesy that would have prevented this.

This isn't a fight. I respect you, and I want you to know that. Kavya, coffee or a call is open whenever you're ready, this week or any time that works for you. I'd genuinely like to talk.

---

Replace "Kavya" with her @ tag so it links to her profile. The draft is about 430 words and roughly 2,500 characters, so it fits both limits.
